newsitem.title: UK: Bagri defends LME, details reforms Exchange wants.
newsitem.headline: Bagri defends LME, details reforms Exchange wants.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange (LME) acted decisively in dealing with the Sumitomo Corp copper affair, and will use the subsequent review of the markets to seek some radical changes, LME Chairman Raj Bagri said.

"The LME has done nothing to be apologetic about. We acted correctly and decisively to deal with a very difficult situation as it unfolded," Bagri said in a speech presented at the LME's annual dinner.

He said that the Daiwa Bank scandal went on for nearly 10 years under stringent U.S. banking regulations, while Metallgesellschaft lost over $1 billiion in oil trading on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX).
"One would have thought that sinners would reflect before preaching the virtues of chastity," Bagri said.

It will take many months before the full facts of the Sumitomo affair are released, but it appears a significant element of the losses were incurred not on the LME, but on over-the-counter (OTC) business.
"The LME will take the opportunity of the Hamanaka affair and the SIB (Securities and Investments Board) review to seek some changes of its own accord."
In June Sumitomo said it had lost $1.8 billion, subsequently revised upwards to $2.6 billion, in 10 years of unauthorised copper trading by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka.

Following this, Bagri asked the SIB, Britain's top regulator, to undertake a review of the market. SIB has since circulated a consultative document to interested parties, who are urged to respond to it, Bagri said.
Even though the LME in its investigations helped to expose the Hamanaka problem the Exchange was completely stunned by Sumitomo's announcement.
"The LME was given no prior notice of its timing or contents by Sumitomo," Bagri said.
The LME chairman said that much of the subsequent criticism of the LME was unfounded, leading to many interested parties exploiting the situation.
These loss-making activities were at the least perpetuated and exacerbated by bank financing, largely outside the UK and via complex derivatives outside LME control.

Bagri had previously warned the metal industry that the massive increase in options and derivatives created the temptation in free markets to build up positions that could result in undesirable situations.
This is the one of the areas that the LME see as ripe for overhaul in the SIB review.

"I do not want to prejudge the findings of the review, though the LME has a 'wish list' of its own in respect to the changes which it will vigorously pursue in regulatory and government circles," Bagri said.

The frustration of investigations into the market could partly be mitigated by the LME being provided with the details of LME members OTC positions, as well as their clients and details of warrant holdings.
Although it would be nice to have jurisdiction over OTC business, this is not easy to achieve.

"We definitely need greater transparency, but this will not be achieved by over-regulation. There is a fine line to be drawn between need and greed and between legitimate surveillance and over-regulation," Bagri said.

The LME would also like to see UK-based entities that actively do LME business be required under Britain's Financial Services Act to be LME members - "removing the opportunity for them to stay outside of the regulatory reach of the LME, the entity which is charged by law to maintain an orderly and proper market," Bagri said.
Additionally, the LME is reviewing the management and Board structure of the Exchange. For the market's credibility the perception of conflict of interests on the Board has to be addressed.
"But it is equally important that those who have the knowledge and experience are not conflicted out on mere apprehension that they will not act honourably."
"An overall increase in the transparency of the market data should help reduce such apprehensions," Bagri said.
